strengths: Novel and intuitive analogy between words/word2vec and events, offering a fresh conceptual framing for representing asynchronous event streams directly as token-like sequences without lossy frame/voxel conversion.

The proposed parametric embedding generation (Algorithm 1) is a reasonably elegant solution to inject neighborhood smoothness into a lookup-table embedding without extra training stages, and the Taylor-expansion argument, while simple, gives an intuitive justification.

Adoption of (bidirectional) linear attention to handle very long event sequences (tens of thousands to over a million events per sample) is a sensible engineering choice given the O(L) memory complexity, addressing a real bottleneck of applying standard Transformers to raw events.

Reported model sizes are considerably smaller than several baselines, and the method uses substantially less processed/training data on ASL-DVS while achieving comparable or marginally better accuracy, suggesting some efficiency benefit.

The paper explicitly discusses forward-looking directions (self-supervised event generation, multimodal integration with LLMs), which, while speculative, is a reasonable framing of significance for the broader community.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is thin: only two datasets are used, and on DVS Gesture the proposed method actually underperforms both baselines (96.01% vs 97.80%/97.92%), undermining the core efficacy claim; on ASL-DVS the improvement over the strongest baseline is marginal (99.80% vs 99.60%) and reported without variance despite averaging over repeated stochastic sampling (16-18 runs), making the significance of the gain unclear.

No ablation studies are provided to isolate the contribution of key design choices: the parametric spatial embedding (Algorithm 1) vs. a plain lookup table, the learned temporal-difference encoding vs. standard positional encodings, or the bidirectional extension of gated linear attention. Without these, it is impossible to verify that the proposed novel components (rather than simply the choice of backbone/hyperparameters) drive the results.

Table 1 comparisons mix very different training regimes (epochs on full converted data vs. partial random sampling with/without replacement) and use a self-defined 'Used Training Data (%)' metric that is not a standard or independently validated measure of data/computational efficiency, making cross-method comparisons potentially misleading.

Missing comparisons to other relevant direct/asynchronous event-processing baselines explicitly discussed in the introduction (e.g., sparse CNNs, AEGNN-style GNNs on DVS Gesture), leaving the empirical positioning of event2vec against the very categories it critiques incomplete.

No latency, throughput, or FLOPs benchmarks are reported despite strong claims about efficiency, low latency, and suitability for edge deployment; only static model size is given, which does not substantiate runtime/energy claims.

The 'first event2vec representation' and novelty claims are not carefully contextualized against existing tokenization-style or patch/graph embedding approaches for event data, so the precise incremental contribution relative to prior token-based event encodings is unclear.

Reproducibility is hampered by an incomplete code link ('available at' left blank) and insufficient detail on some experimental settings (e.g., random augmentation specifics, exact optimizer schedule per dataset, variance of repeated evaluations).

The final Discussion section makes several speculative claims (e.g., 'event-GPT', multimodal fusion with LLMs) without any supporting experiments or even preliminary evidence, which slightly overstates the paper's demonstrated contribution.

strengths: The core framing—drawing an analogy between words/word2vec and events/event2vec to motivate a token-sequence representation of AER streams—is a conceptually interesting way to connect event-based vision with the NLP/LLM toolbox, and could inspire follow-up work on multimodal integration of events with language models.

The proposed parametric embedding generator (Algorithm 1) that produces a locality-preserving embedding table via a differentiable network ϕ is a reasonable and relatively elegant mechanism to inject spatial inductive bias into a lookup-table embedding without extra pretraining or neighbor-averaging overhead.

The paper reports practical efficiency metrics (model size, fraction of training data used) alongside accuracy, which is relevant to the stated motivation of enabling lightweight, low-latency, edge-deployable event processing.

The overall method description (spatial embedding, temporal encoding via timestamp differences, bidirectional gated linear attention backbone) is formalized with equations and is largely reproducible in terms of architectural description.
weaknesses: No ablation studies are provided: the paper never isolates the contribution of the proposed locality-preserving embedding (Algorithm 1) vs. a standard lookup embedding (Eq. 2), nor the benefit of the learned temporal-difference encoding vs. standard positional encodings, nor the bidirectional vs. unidirectional gated linear attention. Without these, it is impossible to verify that the paper's central technical claims (neighborhood semantics help, bidirectional GLA helps) actually translate into measurable gains.

Empirical validation is limited to two small, well-worn datasets (DVS Gesture with only 1176/288 samples, and ASL-DVS). No larger-scale or more diverse event datasets (e.g., N-Caltech101, N-ImageNet, event-based driving datasets) are used to support generality claims about this being a broadly applicable new representation paradigm.

The quantitative results are mixed and not convincingly superior: on DVS Gesture the method underperforms prior work (96.01% vs 97.80–97.92%), and on ASL-DVS the improvement over the strongest baseline is marginal (99.80% vs 99.60%) and reported without variance/confidence intervals despite averaging over repeated stochastic sampling runs, making it hard to assess statistical significance.

Central motivating claims about latency, real-time capability, and GPU-parallel efficiency are never actually measured. No wall-clock training/inference time, throughput, or latency comparisons against baselines are reported, despite these being the headline practical advantages claimed in the introduction and discussion.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, architectures, and training regimes (e.g., "Used Training Data (%)" computed differently for different methods), which makes the efficiency comparisons somewhat apples-to-oranges and potentially favorable to the proposed method by construction.

The theoretical justification for the locality property of the embedding (Eq. 5–6, Taylor expansion argument) is a fairly trivial restatement that a continuous, differentiable function is locally smooth; it does not establish that the learned ϕ in practice acquires meaningful or useful neighborhood semantics, nor is this property empirically verified (e.g., via embedding similarity visualization).
The code/model repository link is missing from the abstract ("available at" with no URL given in the provided manuscript), undermining the stated reproducibility commitment.

The discussion section leans heavily on speculative future applications ("event-GPT," multimodal LLM fusion) without any supporting experiments, which inflates the perceived significance of the contribution beyond what is empirically demonstrated.

The method's practical gain for DVS Gesture required substantial dataset-specific tuning (heavy data augmentation, specific sampling-without-replacement strategy, 18x repeated inference) while still underperforming simpler/more established baselines, raising questions about the robustness and generality of the approach.

strengths: The word-to-event analogy is an interesting conceptual framing that motivates treating events as a token sequence, avoiding lossy conversion to frames/voxels/graphs.

The paper proposes a reasonable engineering pipeline: a hypernetwork-generated spatial embedding table intended to encode neighborhood smoothness, a learned temporal encoding from timestamp differences, and a bi-directional gated linear attention backbone with O(L) complexity suited to very long event streams.

Demonstrates that competitive accuracy can be achieved on ASL-DVS with drastically smaller model size (0.35MB) and far less training data than graph/voxel-based baselines, while avoiding preprocessing latency.
Experimental protocol is described in reasonable detail (hyperparameters, sampling strategy, augmentation, number of repetitions for stochastic inference), aiding reproducibility if code is released.
weaknesses: No ablations isolating the actual contribution of the core proposed components: the parametric hypernetwork-generated embedding (Algorithm 1/Eq. 4) is never compared against the 'trivial' standard embedding (Eq. 2) it is meant to improve upon, so the central technical claim about neighborhood semantics is asserted via a Taylor-series argument but never empirically validated (e.g., no embedding visualization, no probing, no accuracy comparison with/without the parametric scheme).
The bi-directional extension of gated linear attention (Eqs. 9-12) is likewise never ablated against a uni-directional baseline, so its necessity/benefit is unsupported.

Validation is limited to two relatively small, well-worn benchmarks (DVS Gesture, ASL-DVS); no larger-scale or more diverse event datasets (e.g., N-Caltech101, N-ImageNet, optical-flow/driving benchmarks) are used to establish generality of the representation.

On DVS Gesture, the proposed method actually underperforms existing SNN and sparse-GRU baselines (96.01% vs 97.8-97.92%), which undercuts the abstract's claim of 'impressive accuracy'; the paper attributes this to dataset scale without further investigation or mitigation.

A central motivating claim of the paper is computational/latency efficiency from avoiding preprocessing and leveraging massively parallel GPU computation, yet no wall-clock timing, throughput, or FLOP comparisons are reported against baselines to substantiate this.

The 'Used Training Data (%)' metric in Table 1 is an ad hoc, non-standard quantity that conflates epochs and event-sampling ratios across heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, making the efficiency comparison difficult to interpret rigorously; no error bars/variance are reported for this metric or for baseline numbers (which are taken from other papers with potentially different protocols).
Related work on tokenizing/embedding events for transformer-style models is not thoroughly surveyed, weakening the strength of the 'first event2vec' novelty claim.

The discussion section spends considerable space speculating about future applications (event-GPT, multimodal driving) without any supporting experiments, which does not substitute for missing core ablations.
No standard deviation/confidence intervals reported despite averaging over repeated stochastic sampling runs, limiting statistical rigor of the accuracy comparisons.
